title: The Inner-Front Strategy: Destroy from Within
hook: Hiroshi closes the attack deck when the faction map shows a cleaner pressure point inside the coalition.
keyTakeaway: Do not strike a divided opponent from the outside when a real internal contradiction can carry the pressure.
counterintuition: A frontal attack can heal the target by giving its factions one enemy. Expose the real fault line without manufacturing mistrust.
tryThisNow: Map one opponent's real contradiction and the move that would accidentally unify it. Avoid the unifying move first.

breakdown.fastRead: Hiroshi is ready to attack the rival coalition's public platform until the faction map changes his mind. One wing wants budget discipline. Another wants rapid expansion. A public attack would let both sides pose as defenders of the same cause. So he drops the attack deck and surfaces their own contradiction instead: the platform promises both spending cuts and new guarantees by Friday. The inner front works only when the fault line is real. You pressure what already divides the target, and you refuse the cheap thrill of inventing rot.
breakdown.deepRead:
Akira pulls the leaked contradiction file from a plastic sleeve and stops before sending it to every board member. The file shows a real split: one faction promised investors a hiring freeze while another promised managers a new regional office. Akira's first instinct is to accuse them publicly. Then she sees the danger. An outside attack could make both factions deny everything together.

The inner-front strategy begins with diagnosis. Where does the group already distrust itself? Which promise cannot coexist with another promise? Which faction needs a different future to stay loyal? Pressure belongs there, because external force often creates forced cohesion. People who dislike one another may still unite against an outsider who looks unfair.

Do not become the glue.

You are beside Aisha as coalition fracture notes sit beside a protest permit application. Two activist groups are already divided over whether to accept a city compromise. Aisha must decide whether to denounce the whole coalition from the outside or ask a public question that makes the existing tactical disagreement impossible to ignore: will the compromise protect the tenants named in the original demand? She uses the real contradiction and refuses to invent suspicion about motives.

The reversal is moral and practical. If you have to plant lies, impersonate voices, or make ordinary disagreement look like betrayal, the move has turned corrosive. If the group has no real contradiction, pressure from within becomes sabotage. Strategy begins by seeing the fault line; it does not license creating one.
breakdown.fullRead:
It took Fatima three weeks to notice the faction map was the part everyone kept avoiding. The company succession fight looked like a single leadership problem from the outside. The outgoing chief wanted a loyal successor. The product division wanted a builder. Finance wanted someone who would stop new hiring. Every memo used the same words about stability, but the notes underneath pointed in three directions. A frontal challenge would have given them a reason to stand together against an ambitious outsider.

Fatima has to decide whether to attack the succession process or surface the contradiction already inside it. She takes the contradiction packet, removes the gossip, and leaves only the promises that cannot all be true: preserve the old structure, launch two new products, and cut headcount. Then she asks the nomination committee to rank those promises before choosing a candidate. The question does not invent mistrust. It makes concealed disagreement do its own work.

That is the clean version of the inner front. It treats cohesion as something to test, not something to smash blindly. Some groups are held together by a slogan, a shared enemy, a deadline, or a fear of looking divided. If you attack from outside, you may strengthen the very bond you hoped to break. If you reveal the internal tradeoff, members have to choose which loyalty matters most.

Here is the guardrail: would the pressure still be defensible if every document, question, and timing choice were made public afterward? If yes, you are probably surfacing a real contradiction. If no, you may be manufacturing distrust while calling it insight. The difference matters because inner-front work sits close to subversion. It can reveal truth, or it can teach you to rot every room you enter.

Yasmin sees the difference in a supplier alliance trust fracture. In the postmortem, her best move was not to accuse the alliance of cheating. It was to point to the delivery calendar and the private discount letters that already contradicted the alliance's public equal-treatment promise. Once the contradiction was visible, smaller suppliers asked their own questions. Yasmin did not need to whisper that anyone was disloyal. The documents made the fault line speak.

Samir uses the before-and-after version in a committee charter conflict. Before, he tried to win votes by criticizing the committee chair. That only made members defend the chair against an outsider. After, he laid the charter beside the budget request and showed that the committee claimed advisory status while asking for binding spending authority. He has to choose whether to keep attacking personalities or force the charter conflict into the open. The second move is slower, but it does not hand the committee an easy enemy.

Use this sparingly. Some divisions are normal disagreement, and healthy disagreement should not be treated as a wound to exploit. Some organizations serve people who would be harmed if you fracture them for sport. The inner front is for situations where real contradictions are already producing strategic instability and a direct attack would only heal the target. Pressure the contradiction, not the people for the pleasure of watching trust fail.

examples.title: Hiroshi Drops the Attack Deck

planSpec.audience: a reader facing a rival coalition with incompatible promises
planSpec.stakes: a public attack could unify factions that are already strained
planSpec.requiredBeat: The protagonist stops a frontal attack and surfaces a true inconsistency inside the coalition.

examples.scenario: Inside the rival coalition internal split room at 11:37 a.m. "We cannot keep pretending this is neutral," Hiroshi says, with the faction map still unopened. He must decide whether to attack the coalition's platform or ask why its budget wing and expansion wing signed incompatible promises.
examples.whatToDo: Cancel the outside attack and make the coalition answer its own contradiction.
examples.whyItMatters: The factions are already divided; a frontal attack would give them a shared enemy.

examples.title: Akira Removes the Gossip

planSpec.audience: a reader deciding how to use a leaked contradiction responsibly
planSpec.stakes: a true inconsistency could be buried under gossip and look manipulative
planSpec.requiredBeat: The protagonist surfaces real contradiction and refuses to invent suspicion.

examples.scenario: During the board faction contradiction room at 8:48 a.m. The leaked contradiction file crackles in Akira's sleeve as rain hits the office window. She has to choose whether to circulate every rumor or strip the file down to the two board promises that cannot coexist.
examples.whatToDo: Remove rumor, keep the incompatible commitments, and ask the board to reconcile them.
examples.whyItMatters: Pressure is legitimate when it rests on real contradictions, not manufactured mistrust.

examples.title: Aisha Asks the Tenant Question

planSpec.audience: a reader facing a coalition split over tactics
planSpec.stakes: a denunciation could force reluctant allies back together
planSpec.requiredBeat: The protagonist uses a true tactical disagreement rather than planting doubts about motives.

examples.scenario: You are beside Aisha as coalition fracture notes sit under the protest permit. She must decide whether to denounce the whole coalition or ask whether the city compromise protects the tenants named in the original demand.
examples.whatToDo: Ask the concrete tenant-protection question and let the real tactical split become visible.
examples.whyItMatters: The move pressures the existing contradiction without inventing betrayal.

examples.title: Fatima Ranks the Promises

planSpec.stakes: an outsider challenge could make factions defend the same flawed process
planSpec.requiredBeat: The protagonist predicts forced cohesion and reveals incompatible succession promises.

examples.scenario: At the company leadership succession tension room at 10:10 a.m. It took Fatima three weeks to notice the faction map was the part everyone kept avoiding. Before nomination day, she must decide whether to attack the process or force the committee to rank promises that cannot all survive.
examples.whatToDo: Make the committee rank stability, product expansion, and headcount cuts before naming a successor.
examples.whyItMatters: The contradiction becomes the pressure point, so Fatima does not become the enemy that unifies them.

examples.title: Yasmin Lets the Calendar Speak

planSpec.audience: a reader spotting unequal treatment inside an alliance
planSpec.stakes: a broad accusation could look self-serving and heal the alliance
planSpec.requiredBeat: The protagonist surfaces true documents and refuses to invent suspicion.

examples.scenario: Near the supplier alliance trust fracture room at 11:21 a.m. What changes when Yasmin stops arguing and points to the leaked contradiction file? The delivery calendar and private discount letters show the alliance has already violated its equal-treatment promise.
examples.whatToDo: Present the documents and let members ask whether the alliance still honors its stated rules.
examples.whyItMatters: The pressure comes from the alliance's own contradiction, not from Yasmin's accusation.

examples.title: Samir Compares Charter and Budget

planSpec.audience: a reader facing a committee claiming one role while seeking another
planSpec.stakes: personal attack could unify the committee around its chair
planSpec.requiredBeat: The protagonist stops attacking personalities and surfaces a charter conflict.

examples.scenario: Fluorescent light catches the margin notes on the committee charter before Samir speaks. He has to choose whether to criticize the chair again or show that advisory status and binding budget power cannot both be true.
examples.whatToDo: Put the charter and budget request side by side and ask the committee to choose its role.
examples.whyItMatters: The visible conflict replaces a unifying personal attack.

questions.prompt: A rival coalition contains a budget wing and an expansion wing. A public attack would let both sides pose as defenders of the same cause. What should you do first?
choices: Surface the incompatible promises and let the coalition answer its own contradiction.
Attack the coalition's character so both wings feel threatened.
Invent a rumor that makes the wings distrust each other.
questions.explanation: The clean move pressures a real internal contradiction. A character attack may unify the factions, and invented rumor crosses the subversion boundary.

questions.prompt: A leaked board file contains both gossip and two commitments that cannot coexist. You want to stop a bad decision without looking manipulative. Which action fits the inner-front strategy?
choices: Send every rumor because confusion helps.
Strip the file down to the incompatible commitments and ask the board to reconcile them.
Attack the board chair in public before anyone reads the file.
questions.explanation: Real contradiction is enough. Sending rumors manufactures mistrust, while a public attack can create forced cohesion around the chair.

questions.prompt: Two activist groups disagree about accepting a city compromise. You oppose the compromise but know a broad denunciation would push them back together. What should you ask?
choices: Whether the coalition secretly hates its own supporters.
Why every member who disagrees is corrupt.
Whether the compromise protects the tenants named in the original demand.
questions.explanation: The tenant question exposes the real tactical contradiction without inventing corrupt motives. The wrong choices try to fracture people by false or inflammatory claims.

questions.prompt: A succession committee promises stability, product expansion, and headcount cuts. An outsider attack would help the factions defend the process together. What is the better pressure point?
choices: Force the committee to rank the promises before choosing a candidate.
Call every committee member disloyal.
Wait silently and hope the contradiction disappears.
questions.explanation: Ranking exposes the internal tradeoff already present. Personal accusation unifies them, and silence leaves the contradiction unmanaged.

questions.prompt: A supplier alliance publicly promises equal treatment but private letters give one large supplier a discount and better delivery calendar. What is the strongest inner-front move?
choices: Whisper that the alliance leaders are criminals without evidence.
Show the documents and ask members whether the alliance still follows its stated rule.
Publish only an angry statement about unfairness.
questions.explanation: The documents make the alliance's own contradiction visible. Whispering invents rot, and anger alone may let the alliance dismiss the challenge as self-interest.

questions.prompt: A committee claims to be advisory while requesting binding budget authority. Your earlier attacks on the chair only made members defend him. What should change?
choices: Attack the chair harder so the committee feels pressure.
Create anonymous messages implying members are betraying one another.
Compare the charter and budget request so members must choose the committee's real role.
questions.explanation: The charter conflict is the real fault line. More personal attack supplies forced cohesion, and anonymous suspicion is manufactured mistrust.

questions.prompt: You find no real contradiction in a competitor's alliance, but you can make ordinary disagreements sound like betrayals. What is the correct reversal condition?
choices: Stop because the move would manufacture mistrust rather than pressure a real fault line.
Proceed because any fracture helps.
Attack from outside and hope they split later.
questions.explanation: No real contradiction means the inner-front strategy has no ethical base. Manufacturing betrayal is not diagnosis, and an outside attack may unify the target.

questions.prompt: A divided leadership team is already arguing over resource allocation. You want to prevent a harmful plan, but a public insult would make them rally together. What should you do?
choices: Insult the team publicly to prove you are serious.
Ask a resource question that forces the existing tradeoff into the open.
Invent a secret faction because real disagreement is too mild.
questions.explanation: A resource question applies pressure to the real contradiction. Public insult gives them an outside enemy, while inventing a faction corrupts the move.

questions.prompt: A colleague says, "Every group has disagreements, so every group can be fractured." Which response best reflects the limits of the strategy?
choices: All disagreement should be hidden from outsiders.
Any group with disagreement deserves to fail.
Healthy disagreement is not automatically a fault line to exploit.
questions.explanation: The strategy is narrow: pressure real contradictions that matter strategically. Treating normal disagreement as a wound to exploit is the corrosive misread.

reviewCards.front: A rival has factions that dislike each other. What danger does a frontal attack create?
reviewCards.back: It can become the shared enemy that forces the factions back into cohesion.

reviewCards.front: What makes an inner-front pressure point legitimate?
reviewCards.back: It rests on a real contradiction, documented tradeoff, or incompatible promise already inside the target.

reviewCards.front: When should you stop using this strategy?
reviewCards.back: Stop when you must invent suspicion, plant lies, or turn ordinary disagreement into betrayal.

reviewCards.front: How do you pressure a committee claiming two roles at once?
reviewCards.back: Put the two commitments side by side and make members choose which role is real.

reviewCards.front: What is the first diagnostic question for the inner front?
reviewCards.back: Ask what promise, faction, incentive, or fear already divides the target from within.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to identify real internal contradictions and avoid the outside attack that would unify the target.

ifThenPlans.plan: If two factions signed incompatible promises, then ask a question that forces the contradiction into public view.
If a leaked file mixes rumor with real inconsistency, then remove rumor and use only the documented contradiction.
If personal criticism has unified the group, then shift to the charter, rule, or resource conflict inside the group.
If equal-treatment language conflicts with private concessions, then show the documents and let members judge the rule.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one tense group and write two columns: real contradiction and attack that would unify them. Do only the diagnostic work today.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Review one conflict each week and identify whether the target is divided by facts, incentives, loyalties, or merely normal disagreement.

memorableLines.text: The inner front works only when the fault line is real.
Pressure the contradiction, not the people for the pleasure of watching trust fail.
